props.title: It's Always Fair Weather

sections.content: It's Always Fair Weather (1955) represents a fascinating turning point in MGM musicals, arriving as the golden age began to fade. Gene Kelly, Dan Dailey, and Michael Kidd play World War II veterans who promise to reunite in 10 years, only to discover they've grown apart. The film's cynical edge and commentary on post-war disillusionment sets it apart from earlier Kelly vehicles like Singin' in the Rain (1952) and On the Town (1949). Directors Stanley Donen and Gene Kelly innovate with split-screen techniques and experimental dance numbers, including Kelly's famous roller-skate routine and a garbage can lid dance that transforms urban debris into percussion instruments.

sections.content: The film's darker themes reflect changing American attitudes in the mid-1950s. Unlike the optimistic post-war musicals like Easter Parade (1948) or The Pirate (1948), It's Always Fair Weather grapples with broken dreams, corporate manipulation, and the hollowness of television culture. Cyd Charisse's role as a sharp television producer provides commentary on the medium that was stealing cinema's audience. The innovative CinemaScope choreography, particularly in numbers like "Once Upon a Time" and "I Like Myself," shows Kelly and Donen pushing the boundaries of what musical staging could achieve.

While less commercially successful than earlier MGM musicals, It's Always Fair Weather proved highly influential on later works that mixed dance with social commentary, from West Side Story (1961) to All That Jazz (1979). The film's integration of realistic drama with fantasy sequences set a template for modern movie musicals like La La Land (2016). SUBHEAD: The End of Hollywood's Golden Age Musicals

sections.content: By 1955, the lavish MGM musical factory was winding down. It's Always Fair Weather shares DNA with contemporary films like The Pajama Game (1957) and Silk Stockings (1957) that tried to adapt the musical form to changing times. The film's meditation on lost friendship and the passage of time feels particularly poignant given how it marked the end of Kelly and Donen's creative partnership.
